title: Two bright guardians
hookLine: conscience and concern for consequences protect the world

lines: A SCRAPE IN THE PARKING LOT.
cards: A driver backs out in an empty parking lot and scrapes a parked car. Nobody saw. There's no camera.
She could drive away. And yet something stops her hand on the gear shift. Maybe it's a feeling: I'm not someone who does that.
Maybe it's a thought: what happens to them, and to me, if I do? There's no police officer in that moment. Something inside is keeping watch.
The Itivuttaka names two of those inner guards, and calls them bright.

teach.b: Two bright qualities, the Buddha says, protect the world. Which two? Hiri and ottappa.
They're hard to translate. Hiri is often rendered moral shame or conscience: the inward sense that this act is beneath me.
Ottappa is moral dread, or concern for consequences: the outward sense of what this act would do, and how it would look to the wise. One looks in, one looks out.

If these two did not protect the world, the text says, people would no longer honor the bonds that hold families and communities together, not mother, not aunt, not a teacher's wife, and the world would fall into confusion.
But because they guard the world, those bonds are recognized. Notice the word bright. In the early texts, sukka, bright, is used for wholesome qualities, as dark is for unwholesome ones.
These aren't the gnawing, sticky guilt that keeps a person up at night. Hiri and ottappa, as teachers often explain them, look forward, and stop the hand before the harm.
And notice the scale: the world, not just my peace of mind. Look back at the week. Neither coming nor going.
No blame to Cunda. Thus it was said. Just one thing.
Share even the last bite. The moon outshines. Most of them turned toward other people: a smith, a servant, a last bite, a wish for every being.
Today's two guardians keep watch over how people treat each other.

how: Theravada teachers often call hiri and ottappa the guardians of the world (lokapala dhamma), and they are counted among the wholesome qualities in Abhidhamma lists and in many Buddhist teachings on ethics.

o: conscience, an inner sense of shame
guilt that gnaws after a mistake
fear of being caught and punished

games.q: two bright guardians: tap the pairs.
p: the early texts' word for wholesome

s: hiri and ottappa mean the same as lingering guilt
they're called bright; they guard before harm is done, unlike gnawing guilt.
the Itivuttaka says these two protect the world
two bright qualities guard the world: hiri and ottappa.
concern for what an act would do, and how it would look to the wise.

games.q: you've scraped a car in an empty lot. no one saw. according to Itivuttaka 42, what keeps the world from falling into confusion in moments like this?
games.why: the text names two bright inner guardians, hiri and ottappa. without them, it says, the bonds people honor would be forgotten.

practice: Think of a moment this week when something in you said, don't; maybe you listened, maybe you didn't, but recall the voice itself, and notice it wasn't cruel, just clear. Thank it, quietly.
If an old guilt keeps gnawing, notice the difference between that and this bright guard, and let the guilt soften.

wordCard.voice: Hiri, conscience or moral shame. Paired with ottappa, concern for consequences, the two qualities the Itivuttaka says protect the world. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali hiri: moral shame, conscience; paired with ottappa (ओत्तप्प), concern for consequences.

carryVoice: Your line: listen to the small don't. Two bright guards, one looking in, one looking out. That's a week.
